SRC_1: In 1874, six men set off into Colorado’s San Juan Mountains in winter hoping to reach newly discovered goldfields on the other side.
Two months later, only one man emerged from the mountains, and he looked weirdly fed instead of emaciated.
The man was Alfred Packer, also known as the Colorado Cannibal.
On the morning of April 16, 1874, men at Los Piños Indian Agency near Saguache, Colorado saw a distressed man enter their mess hall during a snowstorm.
The man who entered the mess hall was Alfred Packer.
Alfred had rags on his feet, a long beard, a coffee pot hanging from a strap on one side, and a rifle on the other.
General Charles Adams oversaw the agency and had his men help Alfred to a table with food.
Alfred ate so quickly that he threw up.
After several whiskeys, Alfred told the agency men about his journey over the mountains.
Alfred said the others with him had become too exhausted to continue, that he had gotten snow blindness and frostbite, and that he had been left behind to fend for himself.
Alfred said that for months he had eaten rabbits, roots, and rosebuds, and that his experience as a guide got him out alive.
Several months earlier, on November 20, 1873, the party Alfred eventually joined set out from Bingham Canyon in Utah as part of a group of 20.
The travelers were heading to newly found goldfields near Breckenridge in Colorado.
The group met Alfred about 25 miles south of Salt Lake City when they bumped into him during the journey.
Alfred offered his services and claimed he was a guide who knew the territory between Utah and Brackenridge well.
The group agreed to take Alfred with them because they thought a guide would help them.
Alfred actually had no idea where he was going, and he had only worked as a guide for a few months.
As a guide, Alfred often got lost and tended to argue with clients.
Alfred had a reputation for stealing and lying.
When he was younger, Alfred served twice in the Union Army during the Civil War.
Each of Alfred’s Army enlistments lasted only a few months because he had epilepsy and was prone to seizures.
Alfred was honorably discharged both times from the Union Army.
After his discharges, Alfred worked driving horses and other draft animals across the West.
Alfred also worked as a hunter, a range hand, and an odd-job worker for mining companies.
Alfred tried mining in Colorado, but these jobs did not last long because he had a bad attitude and kept getting fired.
SRC_2: Alferd E. Packer lived from 1842 to 1909 and was also called “Alfred.”
Packer was a prospector who became famous after confessing to eating his dead comrades while trapped in the San Juan Mountains in February 1874.
The text says it appears likely that Packer killed another prospector in self-defense before he began gnawing on the corpses of those who had already died.
Packer’s cannibalism story is presented as highlighting the dangers faced by nearly every nineteenth-century prospector who ventured into the Rocky Mountains.
Packer’s story has become one of the West’s most grisly and enduring legends and murder mysteries.
Packer had been part of a larger band of twenty gold seekers who left Utah and split into two groups.
On February 9, 1874, Al Packer and five other prospectors departed the Ute leader Ouray’s winter camp.
The prospectors ignored Ouray’s warning and declined his offer to let them stay before heading into deep snow.
Packer later said that three or four days after their provisions were gone, the men cooked their raw-hide moccasins.
Packer later said that when their trail was drifted over, they gathered wild rose buds, stewed them, and ate them.
Packer left Utah with few provisions and no weapons.
Nine weeks later Packer arrived at the Los Piños Indian Agency south of present-day Gunnison with a Winchester rifle, a skinning knife, and a coffee pot containing live coals.
When he reached the Los Piños Indian Agency, Packer was haggard and worn but otherwise fit.
Packer played high-stakes poker at Dolan’s saloon and bought a $70 horse.
Another member of the original gold seekers questioned where Packer had gotten his spending money.
Packer admitted that the small band had starved in the San Juans, that Israel Swan had died from hunger and exposure, and that Packer had eaten him.
Packer was jailed in Saguache, escaped, changed his identity, and was arrested in Wyoming before being returned to Hinsdale County for trial.
The area northeast of Lake City where Packer’s party got lost is labeled “Cannibal Plateau” on maps.
The site where the bodies were found five miles beyond town is called Deadman’s Gulch.
After being re-captured, Packer said Shannon Bell killed James Humphrey, George Noon, and Frank Miller as they slept around the campfire while the group tried to find the Indian Agency.
Packer said that when he returned from searching for food, Shannon Bell accosted him with a hatchet.
Packer said he fired twice with a pistol and shot Bell in self-defense.
Packer said that after killing Bell he lived on the flesh of the dead men for the greater part of the sixty days he was out.
Packer’s lawyer mounted a spirited defense, but Packer went to prison for seventeen years before The Denver Post petitioned for his release.
In prison, Packer made horsehair bridles, and one is displayed at the Museum of Western Colorado in Grand Junction.
SRC_3: Alfred Griner Packer was born on January 21, 1842, in Allegheny County, Pennsylvania, near Pittsburgh.
Alfred Griner Packer died on April 23, 1907, in Jefferson County, Colorado, at age 65.
Packer was also known as John Schwartze and the Colorado Cannibal.
Packer was known for cannibalism.
Packer’s convictions were murder, which was later overturned, and five counts of voluntary manslaughter.
Packer’s criminal penalty was death, which was commuted to 40 years in prison.
Packer was an American prospector and self-proclaimed wilderness guide.
Packer confessed to cannibalism during the winter of 1874.
The text says no clear or definitive evidence has yet been found to prove Packer’s deeds.
The text says he is one of four people historically convicted for cannibalism in the United States.
Packer emerged as the sole survivor of a six-man party that tried to travel through the San Juan Mountains of the Colorado Territory.
Packer gave more than one version of his account of the circumstances surrounding the deaths of his companions.
After his story was questioned, Packer escaped jail and hid from justice for nine years.
He was eventually tried, convicted of premeditated murder, and sentenced to death.
Packer won a retrial and was eventually sentenced to 40 years in prison on five counts of voluntary manslaughter.
The Legend of Alfred Packer, an almost completely fictitious biopic of his exploits, was released in 1980.
Cannibal! The Musical, a more comedic and heavily fabricated version of the story, was released in 1993.
Packer’s father moved the family to LaGrange County, Indiana, by the early 1850s and worked there as a cabinetmaker.
Packer moved to Minnesota in his late teens and worked as a shoemaker.
Packer enlisted in the Union army on April 22, 1862, in Winona, Minnesota, and was assigned to Company F of the 16th Infantry Regiment.
Packer was honorably discharged eight months later because of epilepsy, which had triggered seizures.
Packer enlisted in the 8th Iowa Cavalry Regiment at Ottumwa, Iowa, on June 25, 1863.
Packer received a second discharge on April 22, 1864, because of epilepsy.
Packer worked as a hunter, wagon teamster, ranch hand, field worker, guide, miner, and other mining-related laborer as he traveled west over the next nine years.
People who knew Packer during this period later said he was ill-suited to being a guide and prone to losing his way.
SRC_4: Alferd Packer was also known as the Colorado Cannibal and was dubbed by local papers the “Man-Eater.”
In the fall of 1873, Packer left with 20 prospectors on an expedition toward San Juan country.
Fierce snowstorms boxed in the party, many of the men returned home, and six men including Packer continued on.
Only Packer returned in the winter of 1874.
The Arrow reported in January 1965 that a blizzard caught the six men without sufficient food and Packer wandered into the Los Pinos Agency in Southwest Colorado three months later.
After a confession, a search for the bodies, and a trial, Packer was sentenced to forty years at the Colorado State Penitentiary.
Packer gave three confessions, in May 1874, March 1883, and August 1897.
In his first confession, Packer said the first two deaths were circumstantial given the rough conditions and that everyone partook in cannibalism to stay alive.
In his first confession, Packer said one man was “killed accidentally” while he was collecting firewood.
In his first confession, Packer said Shannon Bell killed a man he called “California” and that he then killed Bell in self-defense before traveling for 14 days back to civilization.
In his second confession, Packer said the party asked him to go up a nearby hill to see whether he could see anything farther away that would help them navigate.
Packer said that when he returned after a full day of going up and coming back down the hillside, Bell had killed the entire camp and was eating the leg of a man roasted in the campfire.
Packer said Bell rushed at him and he shot Bell through the stomach with the rifle he had taken on the trip up the hillside.
In his 1883 confession, Packer said, “I went back to the fire covered the men up and fetched to the camp the piece of meat that was near the fire.”
In his 1883 confession, Packer said, “I tried to get away every day but could not so I lived off the flesh of these men, the bigger part of the 60 days I was out.”
Packer’s third confession included more details but had largely the same information as the second confession.
District Court Judge Melville Gerry reportedly told Packer at sentencing in 1883, “stand up, Alferd Packer, you voracious, man-eating s– of a b—-.”
Melville Gerry reportedly said, “There were seven Democrats in Hinsdale County, and you ate five of them.”
Melville Gerry reportedly sentenced Packer to hang until he was dead, dead, dead as a warning against reducing the Democratic population of the state.
The Washington Post reported in April 1984 that Judge Gerry made those remarks.
Packer’s death sentence was overturned by the Colorado Supreme Court in 1885 because of a “grandfather clause.”
Packer’s attorney argued that Packer did not get a speedy trial.
Packer’s attorney also argued that the murder indictments came after what was then a statute of limitations of three years.
Packer was resentenced in 1886 to 40 years in prison.
Former Gov. Charles Thomas paroled Packer in 1901.
SRC_5: Alferd Packer, called “The Colorado Cannibal,” is described as one of the most notorious and most misunderstood tales in Colorado history.
Packer was a prospector who headed for Colorado’s gold fields with five other men across the San Juan Mountains in the winter of 1874.
Packer was the only man from that trip who survived.
Packer emerged from the woods with a pocket full of cash and no traveling party, which aroused suspicion.
Packer was accused of murdering the other men.
Packer said the members of his party died one at a time and were eaten by the others until only he and Shannon Bell remained.
In Packer’s account, Bell tried to kill Packer before dying of natural causes so he would not be eaten first.
Packer said Bell was killed in a fight and that he then had no choice but to eat Bell.
Local authorities did not believe Packer’s story.
Packer was charged with murder.
Packer escaped from the Saguache jail.
Packer stayed on the run for eight years before authorities tracked him down.
Packer was found guilty of Bell’s murder in 1883.
Packer was originally sentenced to death.
After a second trial in 1885, Packer received a 40-year sentence.
Packer served 16 years of that sentence before being released.
Packer lived the rest of his life in relative peace.
Packer died peacefully, but his legacy remained unsettled.
The story of Packer has been the subject of historical and popular discussion ever since.
The article says the story known about Packer and the story that actually occurred are not always the same.
The article says the real story of Packer’s crimes, trials, and life can be found at the Western History/Genealogy Department.
A famous quote attributed to Judge M.B. Gerry during Packer’s first trial is presented as likely false.
The attributed quote says Packer should stand up and receive his sentence for eating five of seven Democrats in Hinsdale County.
The attributed quote says Packer should be hanged by the neck until dead as a warning in reducing the county’s Democratic population.
Fred M. Mazzula, in his book Al Packer, A Colorado Cannibal, noted that Judge Gerry did not speak like the exaggerated quote suggests.

SRC_7: More than a century after Alfred Packer was first accused of killing and eating five fellow prospectors in Colorado, forensic law professor James Starrs said Friday that he had proven Packer was “guilty as sin.”
James Starrs described Packer as having “butchered his five fellow prospectors to death” and then skinned them while feasting on their flesh.
Starrs was a professor of law and forensic science at George Washington University.
Starrs led a team of forensic investigators that exhumed the bodies of the five victims from a mass grave in the San Juan mountains last July.
Starrs said the added scientific evidence, in his opinion, convicted Packer beyond any shadow of a doubt.
Packer was one of six prospectors who headed into the Colorado mountains in February 1874 after being flushed with gold fever and ignoring the dangers of winter.
Packer had a reputation as a scurrilous liar and thief.
Packer became the source of legend after he wandered out of the mountains alone in April 1874.
Packer claimed that his five companions had all died or been killed during the harsh winter.
Packer claimed that the survivors ate the flesh of the dead one by one to avoid starvation.
Later that summer, the remains of the five were discovered together.
After the remains were found, Packer’s stories about the adventure began to unravel.
In 1883, Packer was charged with murdering all five companions.
In one confession, Packer admitted shooting one man in self-defense.
According to legend, the Lake City, Colorado, judge who sentenced Packer to death accused him of eating five of the seven Democrats in the county, but historians said that account was apocryphal.
Packer won an appeal on a technicality.
Packer was retried and convicted on involuntary manslaughter charges.
Packer was paroled in 1901 after a Denver Post columnist crusaded on his behalf.
Starrs said that over the years since 1874 Packer had been lionized, apologized for, and sympathized with.
Starrs noted attempts to have Packer pardoned posthumously.
Starrs displayed a T-shirt bearing five skulls and crossed bones with the legend “Gimme Five! The Packer Project.”
Starrs told reporters that Alfred Packer was as guilty as sin and his sins were all mortal.
Starrs said the team’s examination of the victims’ bones showed that none had been shot.
Starrs said four of the victims had been killed by hatchet blows to the head.
Starrs said the fifth skull had not been found.
SRC_8: Alferd Packer survived for weeks in the frozen wilderness by eating his companions, and he admitted that much.
Decades later, details uncovered about the case did not match the official narrative.
On July 17, 1989, grad students dug up skeletons in Lake City, Colorado, while reporters filed a story titled “Professor Exhumes 100-Year-Old Victims of Colorado Cannibal.”
The team led by law professor James Starrs unearthed the skeletons of five men.
The five men were allegedly murdered and partially consumed by Alferd Packer, also called Alfred Packer and the Colorado Cannibal.
Packer was born near Pittsburgh in 1842.
Packer suffered from epilepsy from an early age, and the condition followed him throughout his life.
Packer enlisted in the Union Army during the Civil War but was discharged because of frequent seizures.
After the war, Packer arrived in Utah in 1873.
Late in 1873, Packer joined a group of 20 prospectors headed to southwestern Colorado.
The prospectors were drawn there by news of a gold strike and reports of enormous fortunes.
Travel was slow, and winter arrived early and severely.
By late January, the prospectors had run out of provisions and were eating livestock feed when they reached a Ute Indian encampment.
Chief Ouray gave the men food and shelter and urged them to stay the winter.
Six prospectors, including Packer, chose to continue on despite the warning.
The six men soon lost their way in the San Juan Mountains and became snowbound.
In mid-April, only Packer emerged from the mountains alive.
Packer looked suspiciously well fed and flush with cash when he emerged.
He spent more than $100 on booze and gambling and seemed strangely uninterested in food.
When questioned, Packer gave the first of several contradictory confessions.
In one confession, Packer said, “We ate old man Swann first.”
Packer claimed that the strong ate the weak one by one and left the bodies miles apart.
Packer claimed that only he and Bell remained, and that Bell tried to kill him, so he shot Bell dead.
Packer was arrested on murder charges but escaped before trial.
A traveling illustrator for Harper’s Weekly found the decomposing remains of the five missing prospectors.
SRC_9: Polly Pry was the pen name of Leonel Campbell Ross O'Bryan, who was born in 1857 and died on 16 July 1938.
Polly Pry was a controversial reporter for The Denver Post and later worked as a freelancer in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.
Polly Pry is best known for her connection to the case of Alfred Packer as an investigative reporter.
At age fifteen, Pry eloped to Mexico with a railroad industrialist named George Anthony.
Five years later, Pry left George Anthony and moved to New York to become a reporter.
The New York Times initially rejected Pry, but she obtained a trial assignment on a recent slum fire.
The article Pry wrote about the slum fire earned her a full-time job at The New York Times.
In 1898, Frederick Bonfils hired Pry for the Denver Post.
Pry became the Denver Post's first female reporter.
Pry was a member of the Denver Woman's Press Club.
Pry met Alfred Packer in 1901 while writing an article about the prison where he was incarcerated.
Pry advocated for Alfred Packer in print throughout his trial and helped win his release.
After the trial, Pry was present during a confrontation involving Packer's attorney and the owners of the Post who had hired him.
The owners discovered that the attorney had taken a double payment and demanded that he return the money.
During the confrontation, the attorney W. W. Anderson pulled a gun and shot both men.
As Anderson prepared to shoot again, Pry jumped in front of Harry Heye Tammen and tried to shield him.
Pry stalled Anderson long enough for the police to arrive.
Pry used her skirt to stop the bleeding.
Rumors later circulated that Pry's skirts saved her publishers' lives by slowing bullets from the gun.
When union workers boycotted The Denver Post over her stance on labor issues and immigration, Pry founded her own paper called Polly Pry.
Gunmen later attacked Pry again in her home because of her paper and public stance.
Pry was a strong advocate of free speech.
During World War I, Pry came to the aid of French war orphans.
Two film versions of the Alferd Packer story included Polly Pry.
In Jim Roberson's The Legend of Alfred Packer (1980), Cynthia Nessin portrayed Polly Pry.
SRC_10: Alferd G. Packer, who lived from 1842 to 1907, was accused of committing murder during the winter of early 1874.
Packer led a prospect party of 21 men that departed Bingham Canyon, Utah, on November 8, 1873, hoping to be among the first to locate mining claims in the San Juan region.
The party reached a Ute encampment near present-day Montrose on January 21, 1874, with its food and supplies exhausted.
At the Ute encampment, the party of 21 prospectors split into three factions.
Chief Ouray warned the men about the treacherous winter conditions ahead of them.
Some men paid a trespassing fee to Chief Ouray and camped with the Utes for the rest of the winter.
Others accepted a week's worth of provisions from Ouray and traveled on to the Los Pinos Agency in Saguache County.
The group that traveled to the Los Pinos Agency nearly perished after losing its way in the harsh mountain wilderness.
A third group ignored Ouray's warnings.
Five prospectors with a week's worth of provisions followed Packer on February 9 southeast and then south along the Lake Fork.
The route passed the site that would become the townsite of Lake City within six months.
Nothing was heard from the six prospectors for nearly three months.
Packer arrived alone at the Los Pinos Agency on April 16.
Packer then went on to Saguache.
Packer attracted suspicion in Saguache by spending large sums of money and possessing a rifle that had belonged to one of the missing men.
Packer was arrested and jailed at Saguache.
In August 1874, a prospecting party discovered the bodies of the five missing men.
An illustrator from Harpers Weekly accompanied the discovery party and recorded the scene in visual graphic detail.
The Harpers Weekly coverage riveted national attention on the grisly crime.
Packer escaped from the jail in Saguache and remained a free man for nine years.
Packer was apprehended in Wyoming in 1883 and brought back to Hinsdale County.
Packer was tried in Hinsdale County, found guilty of murder, and sentenced to hang.
Packer appealed for a retrial on the grounds that the crime was committed on the Ute Reservation in early 1874 and should therefore have been subject to federal rather than local jurisdiction.
Packer was incarcerated at Gunnison while awaiting retrial for nearly four years.
While incarcerated at Gunnison, Packer became a local celebrity.
SRC_11: The text describes Alfred Packer as the most celebrated Colorado convict and says he was wooed and loved despite a life sentence for eating his camping companions.
Mental health professionals call the disorder in which women become infatuated with jailed killers and murderers hybristophilia.
Popular culture calls hybristophilia Bonnie and Clyde syndrome.
The condition is usually characterized by a woman communicating with a high-profile criminal in an attempt to kindle a relationship.
The text says hybristophilia was not solely a 20th-century phenomenon.
Alfred Packer, also spelled Alferd, received fan mail from several adoring women while incarcerated for his crimes.
Packer committed cannibalism during the winter of 1874 after guiding a group of five men into Colorado Territory’s San Juan Mountains during a snowstorm.
After arriving alone at the Los Pinos Indian Agency, Packer claimed that his companions had left him while they searched for food.
Packer said he did not know what happened to his companions even though he carried large sums of their money and possessed a rifle that had belonged to one of them.
People who knew Packer questioned his account, and he was soon arrested.
Under interrogation, Packer admitted to partaking in cannibalism but denied committing murder.
After Packer was incarcerated, the mutilated bodies of his five companions were discovered.
Most historians conclude that an illustrator for Harper’s Weekly found the remains near the Gunnison River while on assignment in the area.
The corpses showed intense violence, including skull fractures consistent with hatchet blows.
After that discovery, Packer escaped from jail and remained a fugitive for nearly 10 years.
In March 1883, Packer was found in Douglas, Wyoming, living under the alias John Swartze.
After this arrest, Packer was tried, convicted of murder, and sentenced to death for killing five other persons for their money and a vicious desire for human flesh and blood.
The judge reportedly told Packer, “I sentence you, Alfred Packer, to be hanged by the neck until you are dead, dead, dead.”
Packer avoided execution on a technicality and received a second trial.
At the end of the second trial, Packer was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to 40 years in the Colorado State Penitentiary in Cañon City.
During incarceration, Packer maintained that he was innocent and said he acted only in self-defense when attacked.
The journalist Polly Pry was one of the most prominent women to champion Packer while he was in prison.
Polly Pry was the pen name of Leonel Campbell Ross O’Bryan.
Fellow reporters reportedly nicknamed O’Bryan Polly Pry because she could pry information out of anyone.
Pry first met and interviewed Packer while researching an article about Colorado’s prison system and the Colorado State Penitentiary.
